title: The economic impact of AI: four future pathways
gist: A research-briefing summary bounding AI's macro impact with four modelled scenarios rather than a point forecast: G7 GDP by 2060 ranges from +8% (Breakthrough) to -4% (Disappointment), with a central case of roughly +3.5% US productivity over the next decade and no sustained rise in unemployment. The sharpest signals are that labour-market flexibility — not the size of the productivity gain — separates the good outcome from structural unemployment, and that the bear case is explicitly defined as adoption falling short of what markets have already priced in. This is a public teaser page for a gated report, so the modelled mechanics are summarised rather than shown.

themes.theme: Scenario bounds instead of a point forecast

insights.claim: Oxford Economics declines to publish a single AI macro forecast and instead publishes four modelled pathways for growth, productivity and employment, on the view that the economic impact of AI is currently too contested to settle with one number.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Treat any single-point AI GDP forecast as false precision; position around the scenario spread and the observable levers (adoption rate, productivity pass-through, labour-market flexibility) that move you between branches.
insights.quote: Rather than settle on a single answer, we put bounds around it: four modelled pathways for growth, productivity, and employment.
insights.locator: How artificial intelligence (AI) reshapes the economy

insights.claim: Modelled G7 GDP in 2060 spans a 12-percentage-point range across AI scenarios: 8% higher under an AI Breakthrough scenario versus 4% lower under a Disappointment scenario.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: The downside branch is not merely 'less upside' but an outright level loss versus baseline — AI disappointment is modelled as GDP-destructive, which matters for how much long-duration equity risk premium is justified on AI optimism alone.
insights.quote: By 2060, G7 GDP could be 8% higher in an AI Breakthrough scenario, while a Disappointment scenario may see it fall by 4%.
insights.locator: How artificial intelligence (AI) reshapes the economy

insights.claim: The three alternative AI scenarios are built by varying a common set of new 'AI scenario levers' covering adoption, productivity gains and labour market outcomes, making the scenarios parameterised rather than narrative.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Gives a checklist of three observable variables to track — adoption pace, measured productivity, and labour absorption — so incoming data can be mapped to a specific branch rather than to vague sentiment.
insights.locator: We model three alternatives: Breakthrough, Disruption

themes.theme: Central case: gradual diffusion, ~3.5% US productivity

insights.claim: The central case assumes AI diffuses steadily rather than abruptly, raising US productivity by around 3.5% over the next decade.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: A ~3.5% cumulative decade-long productivity uplift is roughly 0.35pp a year — materially below the transformational narratives embedded in AI equity valuations, so the base case is closer to 'useful' than 'revolutionary'.
insights.quote: In our central case, AI diffuses steadily rather than abruptly, raising US productivity by around 3.5% over the next decade
insights.locator: In our central case, AI diffuses steadily

insights.claim: In the central case the pace of AI diffusion is slow enough that labour markets adjust without a sustained rise in unemployment, so the productivity gain lifts growth without a technological unemployment shock.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Argues against positioning for an AI-driven unemployment spike in the base case; a sustained rise in unemployment would itself be the signal that the economy has shifted off the central path.
insights.locator: enough to lift growth, but slow enough

themes.theme: Labour-market flexibility as the swing variable

insights.claim: Breakthrough and Disruption assume comparable productivity gains and differ mainly in labour-market flexibility: flexible markets absorb the shift, while rigid ones generate structural unemployment from the same technological gain.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: The key non-obvious claim: the size of the AI productivity gain does not determine the employment outcome — labour-market institutions do. Watch hiring frictions, retraining policy and employment protection by country, not just capability benchmarks.
insights.quote: Disruption delivers comparable productivity gains into rigid labour markets, generating structural unemployment.
insights.locator: Breakthrough pairs rapid adoption with labour markets

insights.claim: Rapid AI adoption is treated as a necessary but insufficient condition for the best macro outcome, since Breakthrough requires rapid adoption paired with labour markets flexible enough to absorb the shift.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Implies the top-quartile macro outcome accrues to economies with both fast adoption and flexible labour, a narrower set than the fast-adopter list alone — a country-selection filter for equity and rates exposure.
insights.locator: Breakthrough pairs rapid adoption with labour markets

themes.theme: Market pricing already embeds an above-baseline AI outcome

insights.claim: The Disappointment scenario is defined explicitly relative to market pricing — adoption and productivity gains falling short of what markets have already priced in — implying financial markets currently discount an AI outcome better than the modelled central case.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: If the bear case is simply 'reality meets the central forecast', then current asset prices carry asymmetric downside; consider hedging AI-levered exposure against a mere normalisation rather than a collapse.
insights.quote: Disappointment sees adoption and productivity gains fall short of what markets have already priced in.
insights.locator: We model three alternatives: Breakthrough, Disruption

insights.claim: Recent financial market swings are cited as evidence of how wide the uncertainty band around the central AI view remains, framing AI-related volatility as repricing between scenarios rather than noise.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Reads AI-equity drawdowns as the market moving probability mass between Breakthrough and Disappointment — useful for interpreting volatility as an implied scenario-probability signal rather than a technical event.
insights.quote: Recent financial market swings are a reminder of how wide the range around that view remains.
insights.locator: Recent financial market swings are a reminder

themes.theme: Uneven global distribution of AI gains

insights.claim: AI's economic gains are modelled as unevenly shared, with the G7 — the most exposed to the technology — gaining the most and economies with weaker digital connectivity such as India gaining considerably less.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Cuts against the leapfrogging narrative for emerging markets: AI is modelled as a developed-market convergence-widener, arguing for DM over weak-connectivity EM exposure on the AI theme.
insights.quote: The G7, most exposed to the technology, stands to gain the most; economies with weaker digital connectivity, such as India, considerably less.
insights.locator: AI’s gains will not be evenly shared

insights.claim: Every AI scenario is run through the Global Economic Model to quantify divergence across every covered economy and indicator, asset returns included.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Scenario-conditional asset return paths are the tradeable output here — the deliverable is a mapping from AI adoption assumptions to cross-country return dispersion, not just a GDP number.
insights.locator: Running every scenario through our Global Economic Model

themes.theme: Adjacent research signals flagged on the page

insights.claim: Companion research summarised on the same page argues China’s low-cost AI models are narrowing the US AI moat and reshaping competition, framed as a bid to deflate US AI valuations.
insights.speaker: Oxford Economics
insights.so_what: A distinct valuation-compression channel from the macro scenarios: even in a high-adoption world, cheap Chinese models could transfer the surplus from US AI incumbents to users.
insights.quote: China’s low-cost AI models are narrowing the US AI moat, reshaping competition
insights.locator: The moat illusion – China’s bid to deflate

insights.claim: Companion research summarised on the same page finds that equity rallies in Taiwan and South Korea have not boosted household consumption, described as a missing wealth effect.
insights.speaker: Oxford Economics
insights.so_what: Weakens the transmission assumption that AI-driven equity gains feed through to Asian domestic demand — argues against playing the AI rally via North Asian consumer names.
insights.quote: Equity rallies in Taiwan and South Korea haven't boosted household consumption
insights.locator: Asia Pacific: From AI rally to consumption
